title: Cursor confirms a stolen Fireworks AI key let attackers ship a backdoored Claude Code extension
subtitle: The AI coding editor's post-mortem says up to 5,000 developers who requested specific cached extension versions on October 29 may have received a trojanized Claude Code build that installed persistent SSH backdoors.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Cursor's updated post-mortem, surfaced in security coverage on November 15 and 16, explains how a stolen access key triggered one of the year's clearest AI developer-tooling supply-chain compromises. The company had issued the key to Fireworks AI, a model-hosting partner. When Fireworks was breached, that key was exposed, and attackers used it to pull data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor shared with Fireworks. From there they reached an internal credential and, on October 29, 2026, pushed trojanized Claude Code extension builds — versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 — into the cache serving Cursor's extension marketplace.

The malicious builds were live for about eleven hours. Cursor says at most 5,000 users who requested those specific cached versions during the window could have received them. The payload tried to add an attacker-controlled SSH key and open a reverse tunnel, giving persistent remote access. Security researchers found implementation errors that likely prevented the backdoor from working on many Windows and macOS systems where SSH wasn't already enabled. Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was not affected, and neither the VS Code Marketplace nor Open VSX Registry was compromised. Affected developers must update to 2.1.314 or later and run Cursor's cleanup scripts — reinstall alone is not sufficient.

This is the second major AI dev-tool supply-chain story of the quarter, after the LiteLLM compromise CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in September, and the Microsoft LiteLLM Python breach in late October. The pattern is consistent: an AI-era product has unusually broad API-key relationships with upstream vendors, a vendor is breached, and the resulting keys unlock marketplaces and build systems that reach thousands of developers at once. The read-only bucket was the pivot point, and marketplaces served cached binaries without re-validating signatures.

A note for learners: in AI tooling, trust boundaries compound. Your editor trusts its marketplace, which trusts its cache, which trusts a vendor key, which trusts a partner's security posture. Each hop looks fine in isolation, but the chain is only as strong as the weakest link. If you ship or depend on AI developer tooling, two habits do most of the work: rotate vendor keys on a schedule, and require signature re-verification at every cache boundary — not only at publish.
